Roller Coaster Physics: Energy & Motion

Interactive investigation • General Curriculum Physics • Grades 11–12 • 45–60 minutes

Use the track photographs to estimate heights, apply conservation of mechanical energy, and analyze the ball's motion after it exits the track.

Student information & learning targets

Learning targets

  • Estimate vertical height using a ruler visible in a photograph.
  • Describe how gravitational potential energy changes along a track.
  • Use conservation of mechanical energy to predict speed.
  • Calculate average speed from video timing and a measured distance.
  • Identify experimental uncertainty and compare measured and predicted results.

Background & equations

As a ball rolls down a track, gravitational potential energy is converted into kinetic energy. In an ideal model, total mechanical energy is conserved. In a real setup, friction, rolling resistance, sound, and other effects transfer some mechanical energy to the surroundings.

Gravitational potential energyPE = mgh
Kinetic energy (translational)KE = ½mv²
Mechanical energyME = PE + KE
Average speedv = distance ÷ time

Use g = 9.8 m/s². Convert centimeters to meters by dividing by 100. For the prediction calculations, assume the ball starts from rest at Point A and use the simplified model that ignores rotational energy and friction. This gives an ideal estimate, not a perfect real-world prediction.

Measurement reminder: Use the ruler markings in the photographs as a scale. Measure vertical height above the tabletop/base level to the center of the ball's path. The images are perspective views, so measurements are estimates. Record to the nearest 0.5 cm where possible. Follow the same track rail shown in the video.

Part A – Photograph investigation: measure the heights

Examine the four photographs. Identify the path followed by the ball. Use these locations in your measurements:

  • Point A – Start: ball release location at the top of the ramp.
  • Point B – Bottom: lowest point reached during the first descent.
  • Point C – Raised section: highest point on the next raised portion of the track, if the ball travels along that route.
  • Point D – Exit: location where the ball leaves the track.

If a point is hard to identify, compare all views. The photos show multiple rails; do not combine measurements from different paths. Use the actual route followed in the video.

Part B – Predict speed using conservation of energy

Enter the mass of the ball in kilograms. Use the measured mass if provided by your teacher.

For a ball released from rest at A, the simplified energy equation is:

mghA = mgh + ½mv²   →   v = √[2g(hA − h)]

Mass cancels when calculating ideal speed. If a point is higher than A, the simple release-from-rest model cannot predict the ball reaching it.

Part E – Analysis questions

  1. At which point is the ball's gravitational potential energy greatest? Explain using height.
  2. At which point would the ball have its greatest kinetic energy in the ideal model? Explain.
  3. Describe the energy transformation as the ball moves from Point A to Point B.
  4. Why does the ball slow down or fail to reach the same height on a later section in a real experiment?
  5. How would the predicted speed at Point D change if the starting height at Point A were increased? Explain.
  6. Why does the mass of the ball cancel from the simplified speed equation? Does that mean mass is irrelevant to every aspect of the real motion?
  7. Identify two sources of uncertainty in measuring heights from the photographs.
  8. Identify two sources of uncertainty in determining the time or distance from the video.
  9. What is the difference between instantaneous speed and average speed? Which one did you calculate in Part C?

Part F – Conclusion

Write one paragraph explaining how energy is transferred as the ball moves along the roller coaster. Use at least two of your measured heights, one calculated ideal speed, and your video-based average speed. State whether your results support conservation of mechanical energy and explain any differences.
